grammar.title: Hvar? · Hvert?
grammar.rule: Hvert? Inn í fjósið. · Hvar? Í fjósinu. · Hjá afa. · Að fjósinu. · Frá fjósinu.
grammar.note_en:
Case is the form of a noun or pronoun that shows its job in the sentence. You already know the nominative for subjects and the accusative for objects. This chapter adds the dative for location and after certain prepositions. A preposition is a short word such as í “in/into”, á “on/onto”, hjá “beside/with”, frá “from”, or að “to/towards”.

Í and á take two different cases. For a location, answering Hvar? “Where?”, use the dative: Kýrin stendur í fjósinu “The cow stands in the cowshed”; Gull er á þakinu “There is gold on the roof”; Á sætunum sitja þrír menn “Three men sit on the seats”. For a destination, answering Hvert? “Where to?”, use the accusative: Kýrin fer inn í fjósið “The cow goes into the cowshed”; Guðrún fer inn í baðstofuna “Guðrún goes into the communal room”; Hann fer inn í höllina “He goes into the hall”. In these sentences the movement crosses into the named place. The same place then has a dative form when the person or animal is there: Nú er hann í höllinni “Now he is in the hall”. A verb of movement alone does not determine the case: the question is whether the phrase gives a destination or the place where the action happens.

Learn each noun's forms rather than attaching one ending to every word. The definite article, the part corresponding to English “the”, is joined to the end of the noun. Compare fjósið → fjósinu “the cowshed”, baðstofan → baðstofunni “the communal room”, lampinn → lampanum “the lamp”, and þakið → þakinu “the roof”. These are singular dative forms. In the plural, the nouns in this chapter have dative -um, with the article -unum: sæti → sætunum “the seats”, göngin → göngunum “the passage”. Göng is grammatically plural even though English normally uses singular “passage”. The change is not simply an extra syllable added to the nominative: the noun's own ending may change as well.

Hjá, frá and að take the dative in their uses here. Hjá tells us who or what someone is beside: Siggi situr hjá afa “Siggi sits beside Grandfather”; Þórunn situr hjá rokknum “Þórunn sits beside the spinning wheel”. Frá marks the starting point: Hann fer frá Helgu “He goes away from Helga”; Bjarni dregur hey frá hlöðunni “Bjarni drags hay from the barn”. Að marks an approach: Ásta fer að fjósinu “Ásta goes towards the cowshed”; Gylfi fer að sætunum “Gylfi goes up to the seats”. Notice that að still has the dative even though it describes movement. The location/destination contrast applies specifically to prepositions such as í and á; it is not a rule that all movement takes the accusative. Names change too: Bjarni → hjá Bjarna “beside Bjarni”, Guðrún → hjá Guðrúnu “beside Guðrún”, Helga → frá Helgu “from Helga”, afi → hjá afa “beside Grandfather”.

The adverbs also distinguish movement and place. Inn means “in” as a direction: Siggi fer inn í fjósið “Siggi goes into the cowshed”. Inni means “inside” as a place: Nú er hann inni í fjósinu “Now he is inside the cowshed”. Similarly út means “out” as a direction and úti “outside” as a place: Siggi fer út í göngin “Siggi goes out into the passage”; Nú stendur hann úti á túninu “Now he stands outside on the home field”. Compare the earlier upp/uppi and niður/niðri. Hvert fer kýrin? asks where the cow is going; Hvar er hún nú? asks where she is now.

Kveikja á is a fixed combination meaning “light” or “switch on”: Guðrún kveikir á lampanum “Guðrún lights the lamp”. It takes á plus the dative; it does not mean movement onto a lamp. Learn kveikir as the supported story form for now. The chapter continues to use third-person verbs: Siggi les hægt “Siggi reads slowly”, Helga les hátt “Helga reads aloud”. Hægt describes speed; hátt describes volume, so they are not opposites. The forms for “I” and “you” come next.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Í baðstofunni sefur fólkið um nóttina. Um kvöldið situr það þar og vinnur.
Guðrún prjónar, Þórunn situr hjá rokknum, og Helga les. Ásta segir: „Í baðstofunni er saga.“ Siggi segir: „Og afi!“
words_with_history.note_en: Baðstofa originally meant a bathing room. On a nineteenth-century turf farm it was the communal living and sleeping room. Beds lined its walls; in winter the household worked and listened to reading there.

pronunciation_note.rule: Ð sounds like th in English this; þ sounds like th in thin.
pronunciation_note.note: Compare voiced ð in baðstofa and Óðinn with voiceless þ in þak.
